bib.title: A Survey on Retrieval And Structuring Augmented Generation with Large Language Models

legacy_report:
SOURCE: "A Survey on Retrieval And Structuring Augmented Generation with Large Language Models", Pengcheng Jiang* (first author), Siru Ouyang* (equal contribution), Yizhu Jiao, Ming Zhong, Runchu Tian, Jiawei Han (all UIUC). Venue stated: KDD '25 (31st ACM SIGKDD, Toronto, Aug 3-7 2025), doi 10.1145/3711896.3736557; arXiv 2509.10697v1 posted 12 Sep 2025. So it is a conference paper, not a bare preprint. The extraction also carries a CC BY 4.0 licence line.

COVERAGE: 15 of 15 pages. The extraction is 122,478 chars. I read the body in full, from the title through the Conclusions and Acknowledgment (about the first 44k chars), and the reference list through roughly ref [77]. The remaining references I did not read, because they are bibliography only. The text extracted cleanly.

CLAIMS (ranked; the paper reports almost no experiments or numbers of its own. It is a map, not evidence.)
1. Proposed (not evaluated) RAS loop: a taxonomy-enhanced retriever fetches thematically and semantically relevant docs, they are structured into a subgraph that updates a query-specific evolving KG, and the LLM emits a focused subquery conditioned on the KG to trigger another retrieval round until knowledge is sufficient.
 number: none
 setup: conceptual design (Fig. 1, Sec 5.1); no experiment, dataset or model.
 quote: "These doc- uments are structured into a subgraph, which updates a query- specific evolving KG." and "the LLM generates a focused subquery conditioned on the KG, initiating another retrieval cycle until sufficient knowledge is gathered."
 where: p.5 (Sec 5.1, end), Fig. 1 on p.4
2. Plain RAG limitation as the survey frames it: it processes unstructured passages, those passages hold non-atomic information that can mislead the LLM, and multi-hop or domain-organised queries are hard for it.
 number: none
 quote: "they typically process unstructured text passages without leveraging structured knowledge, contain non-atomic information that can mislead LLMs [50, 95, 261], and struggle with complex queries requiring multi-hop reasoning"
 where: p.1 (Sec 1)
3. Graph-based retrieval replaces chunk similarity. The survey cites HippoRAG (LLM triple extraction, then personalized PageRank around query entities to find passages with implicit connections), KG-RAG (Chain of Explorations traversal, claimed higher precision than vector retrieval), GFM-RAG (a pre-trained query-dependent graph foundation model, multi-hop in one step), and Xu et al. (issue tickets parsed to trees, entity match and traversal instead of chunk similarity).
 number: none (no figures given for any)
 quote: "HippoRAG [ 68] constructs a KG from passages using LLM-based triple extraction, then leverages person- alized PageRank [73] to explore graph neighborhoods around query entities to identify relevant passages with implicit connections."
 where: p.4-5 (Sec 5.1)
4. RL-trained query rewriting. DeepRetrieval optimises retrieval metrics (Recall@K, NDCG) directly; s3 trains a search-only agent with a generation-aware reward and needs far less training data.
 number: 3B parameters
 setup: self-reported by the survey from Jiang et al. [92], across literature, evidence-seeking and SQL retrieval tasks; the survey gives no benchmark table.
 quote: "achieves SOTA perfor- mance across literature, evidence-seeking, and SQL retrieval tasks with only 3B parameters."
 where: p.3 (Sec 3.2.3)
 related quote: "using a generation-aware reward rather than search-only metrics—can yield strong downstream improvements while requiring orders of magnitude less training data."
5. Sparse retrieval remains a competitive baseline, especially with limited training data or in a specific domain. Dense retrieval beats BM25 on open-domain QA (DPR) but depends on large labelled data and is hard to interpret.
 number: none
 quote: "it remains a strong baseline due to its effectiveness, efficiency and interpretabil- ity. It continues to be competitive with more complex neural mod- els, particularly with limited training data or domain-specific con- straints [238]."
 where: p.2 (Sec 3.1.1; the sentence starts "Even in the deep learning era, sparse retrieval")
6. Hybrid retrieval combines sparse and dense (CLEAR learns a dense residual to complement BM25; Luan et al. fuse sparse and dense) for effectiveness and robustness.
 number: none
 quote: "Luan et al. [150] explicitly combined sparse and dense representations, achieving better ranking accuracy than strong single-method baselines."
 where: p.3 (Sec 3.2.1)
7. Two-stage retrieve-then-rerank. BERT rerankers "dramatically improve" ranking, and LLMs are now state-of-the-art rerankers.
 number: none
 quote: "Nogueira and Cho [182] demonstrated BERT-based rerankers dramatically improve ranking quality."
 where: p.3 (Sec 3.2.4)
8. RAG vs fine-tuning, and long context. RAG "consistently outperforms" fine-tuning for existing and new knowledge (cited from Ovadia et al. [193]). RAG stays relevant despite long context windows because of efficiency, transparency and domain adaptability.
 number: none
 quote: "Recent evaluations reveal that while fine- tuning shows some improvement, RAG consistently outperforms it for both existing and new knowledge [ 193]."
 where: p.2 (Sec 2.2.3)
9. Structure-summarisation approaches such as GraphRAG: hierarchical community detection, then a map-reduce over community summaries, which suits queries that need global corpus understanding. KARE does selective community retrieval.
 number: none
 quote: "Its map-reduce approach gener- ates partial answers from relevant community summaries before ag- gregating them into comprehensive responses, effectively handling queries that require global corpus understanding."
 where: p.6 (Sec 5.2.2)
10. Taxonomy-guided retrieval (ToTER, TaxoIndex) improves domain-specific dense retrieval without large labelled data, and retrieval quality varies by query taxonomy class (Lima et al.).
 number: none
 quote: "performance varies significantly across different query taxonomy classes, reinforcing the importance of structured categorization for optimizing retrieval."
 where: p.4-5 (Sec 5.1)
11. Generative retrieval claim: at equal parameter size and training data it can perform better and be more interpretable. This is attributed to cited work and unquantified.
 quote: "Given the same parameter size and training data, GR can achieve better performance [ 236, 252] and interpretability [236, 290]"
 where: p.3 (Sec 3.1.3)
12. Extraction caveat: LLMs show limits in relational reasoning, and triple-extraction quality is a risk.
 quote: "However, LLMs show limitations in relational reasoning, possibly due to the scarcity of RE tasks in instruction- tuning datasets"
 where: p.3 (Sec 4.1.3); Sec 6.1.2 also says automated structuring "can introduce noise or inconsistencies"

LIMITS
- It is a survey with no experiments, benchmark table, ablation or cost figure of its own. Every performance statement is qualitative and borrowed from cited papers. The RAS loop in Fig. 1 is explicitly a proposal and was never run.
- It does not compare structured retrieval against hybrid chunk retrieval, and gives no latency or indexing-cost numbers. Sec 6.1.1 only lists retrieval efficiency as an open challenge.
- Its own future-work list (Sec 6): retrieval efficiency, knowledge quality and noise, integration and conflict resolution, multimodal, cross-lingual, self-refining, human-AI, personalised.
- Dated: the coverage ends around early 2025 (it cites DeepSeek-R1 and s3). Its section on KG-embedded LLMs (GraphToken, G-Retriever) is about training, which needs open weights.
- A few citations look wrong. Ref [48] "Self-Refine" lists different authors, and ref [66] is a PaLM 2 blog post used to support "robust validation techniques". Do not cite the survey for those.

BUILDS ON (as printed)
Lewis et al. 2020 / Gao et al. 2023 (RAG and the RAG survey, naive / advanced / modular paradigms), Karpukhin et al. DPR, Khattab ColBERT, Formal et al. SPLADE 2021, Gao et al. CLEAR ECIR 2021, Nogueira & Cho (BERT reranking), Edge et al. 2024 GraphRAG, Gutierrez et al. HippoRAG NeurIPS 2024, Sun et al. ToG, Asai et al. Self-RAG 2023 (adaptive retrieval), Jiang et al. DeepRetrieval and s3 (the same first-author group), Ma et al. 2023 Rewrite-Retrieve-Read, and Han's group work on taxonomies (TaxoGen, TELEClass, ToTER, TaxoIndex).

CODE: none. The paper has no code.

FIGURES
- Fig. 1, p.4: "An abstractive example of RAS paradigm." It shows the Query to Taxonomy Retriever to Thematically & Semantically Relevant Text to Structuring to Subgraph to KG to LLM loop, with a Feedback & Subquery arrow back to retrieval. It is the quickest picture of an iterative retrieval-and-structuring loop. It is the only figure.

PROBLEMS: none that block use. Extraction is clean, and the text had no embedded instructions. Quotes contain extraction hyphen-breaks ("person- alized") copied as extracted.

NOTE FIT (generative-ai/02-rag-retrieval/notes/01-rag-pipeline.md)
- Strongest point for that note: query-time structuring and graph retrieval, meaning the Fig. 1 loop (retrieved text becomes a query-specific evolving KG, and the LLM's KG-conditioned subquery drives the next retrieval) plus HippoRAG-style personalized PageRank retrieval.
- It bears on two sections. The first is "Index-time structures: RAPTOR, GraphRAG, filesystems", at lines 397-432. The second is "Agentic RAG", around line 433.
- The note does not say it yet. That section covers only index-time structure: RAPTOR, GraphRAG with community summaries, filesystem L0/L1/L2, and knowledge discovery. It has no query-time evolving graph, no personalized PageRank or HippoRAG, no taxonomy-guided retrieval, and no GFM-RAG or KG-RAG. A grep of the notes folder for HippoRAG, DeepRetrieval, taxonomy-guided retrieval and "Jiang 2025" found nothing. The only "taxonomy" hits are the note's own classifier spec in 10-semantic-cache.md and the Zhao query-level taxonomy in 02.
- The rest is sharpens-level, with no new claim:
  - the naive / advanced / modular paradigms (note 01 already cites Gao et al.);
  - sparse as a strong baseline plus hybrid (03);
  - rerank (05);
  - RAG vs fine-tuning (02, which already has the Balaguer paper);
  - GraphRAG map-reduce over communities (the note already covers GraphRAG).
- DeepRetrieval and s3 (RL-trained query rewriting) could go in the pre-retrieval pipeline section of 01 or in 05 (query parsing). The note does not cover them, and the survey gives no numbers, so cite them as pointers only and take figures from the primary papers.
- Caveat for the ledger: the survey gives no evidence, so cite it as a map (as the note already does for the Zhao and Tonmoy surveys) with the "no experiments" qualifier.
